acilis-bilgi: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk said these words while the country was under enemy occupation. Six months later he landed at Samsun and took the first step towards liberation. This map tells that journey through its turning points, from 16 May 1919 to 29 October 1923.
acilis-kimden: Mustafa Kemal, Istanbul, 13 November 1918 · “Geldikleri gibi giderler.”
acilis-soz: They will leave just as they came.

hk-giris: The turning points and journeys of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk from his departure from İstanbul on 16 May 1919 to the proclamation of the Republic on 29 October 1923.
hk-kaynaklar-liste:
• Gazi Mustafa Kemal, Nutuk (The Great Speech; full text: National Defence University, Turkish Military Academy).
  • The words on the opening page were spoken by Mustafa Kemal on his return to Istanbul on 13 November 1918 and have come down to us through the memoirs of those with him; the English translation was made for this site.
  • Atatürk Ansiklopedisi, Atatürk Araştırma Merkezi (ataturkansiklopedisi.gov.tr).
  • For the dates of intermediate stops also: Ö. Toraman, Vakanüvis 8 (Özel Sayı), 2023; O. Akandere, Atatürk Araştırma Merkezi Dergisi.

hk-nasil-liste:
• The map opens in İstanbul, where the journey began; tapping "Start the journey" or the ship opens the map out to Turkey and brings up the card of the first stop. The map shows the turning points of the period and the journeys connecting them; the account and photographs for each stop are in the stop card.
  • "Continue the journey" at the bottom of the card moves to the next stop, and the route is drawn on the map as you go; "Previous stop" goes back. Tapping the icon of a place already visited on the map also goes to that stop. On a phone the card has three sizes: pulling the handle up or tapping "Read more" opens it fully, pulling it down leaves only a strip with the title.
  • The icon of the current stop is outlined with a thin orange line and shown in full colour, earlier ones faded; the most recently drawn route is the most prominent. Where a city has several stops, only the latest one is shown on the map.
  • The colour of a route shows how he travelled; each card says so under "How he got here". The route colours come from the colour-blind friendly Okabe-Ito palette; where the sources do not say how he travelled, the line is grey. The legend button at the top left explains the icons and colours.
  • The "Watch the journey" button with the mountain icon, the last of the buttons at the top left, plays the whole journey in 3D from the beginning: a vehicle moves along the route, the camera follows it from behind and at each stop looks from the direction of arrival; at each stop one or two narrated sentences tell what happened there while a model marking the event appears. Zooming in with the + and − buttons or the mouse wheel makes the vehicle smaller and slower; zooming out makes it larger and faster. Dragging with the right mouse button (two fingers on a phone) changes the viewing angle; dragging with the left button pauses playback, and the play button brings the camera back to the vehicle. Where the means of travel is unknown, the vehicle is semi-transparent.
hk-yollar-metin: The roads of those years no longer exist; the lines follow today's road and railway equivalents of the same route. Sea routes are approximate. The steamer, car and train in the 3D view are models evoking the vehicles of the period, and the buildings and objects at the stops are representations; a vehicle's position on the route is estimated from the start and end dates of the journey.
lejant-not: Lines follow today's equivalent of the route. The emphasised line is the latest journey; faded lines are earlier routes.
